chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halaby, who said:
There is no problem if a man were to recite the Azan without being in ablution, but he cannot recite the Iqamah unless he is upon ablution.

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: there is no problem / it is permissible
key_terms.يُؤَذِّنَ: to recite the Azan (call to prayer)
key_terms.يُقِيمُ: to recite the Iqamah (call to establish prayer)

ai.seo_question: Is ablution required for Azan and Iqamah?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated via the chain of Hammad ibn Uthman al-Halabi, clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between the Azan and Iqamah by exempting the former from the requirement of ritual purity while maintaining it for the latter. In Shia fiqh, this ruling underscores the view that the Azan is a declaration rather than an act of worship requiring a specific state of purity, whereas the Iqamah is closely linked to the immediate commencement of the prayer. This distinction highlights the practical flexibility in the call to prayer while preserving the sanctity associated with the formal establishment of the congregational prayer.
